title: Insect floral visitors and reproductive biology of Chinese tallow (Triadica sebifera: Euphorbiaceae): a multi‑state study in the southeastern United States
content:
Abstract
Chinese tallow (Triadica sebifera: Euphorbiaceae) is a tree native to southern China that was introduced to the United States in 1776 to establish a soap industry. Since then, it has escaped cultivation and become a widespread invasive species in the southeastern United States. Although its spread is well documented, little is known about the native pollinators that visit its flowers or its reproductive biology across a broad geographic scale. The objectives of this study were to (i) characterize insect floral visitors of Chinese tallow in the southeastern United States (ii) assess how insect abundance and richness vary among inflorescence bloom types (staminate, pistillate, and synchronous), and (iii) evaluate tallow’s reliance on insect pollination using an exclusion experiment. Pollinator surveys were conducted during spring bloom periods in 2021 and 2022 across Alabama, Florida, Mississippi, and Louisiana, with insect exclusion experiments completed in Alabama and Florida in 2022. We documented 1,079 pollinating insects representing 38 families and 177 genera/species. Insect abundance and community composition differed among bloom types, with several taxa captured significantly more often on staminate inflorescences than pistillate inflorescences. Exclusion experiments demonstrated that Chinese tallow is highly dependent on biotic pollination for fruit and seed production. Overall, Chinese tallow attracts a diverse assemblage of insect visitors, particularly pollinators in the genera Bombus, Lasioglossum, Palpada, and Xylocopa. This attraction may divert pollinator visitation away from native plants, potentially reducing native plant reproduction and disrupting plant–pollinator networks, posing a risk to ecosystem stability and biodiversity in the southeastern United States.
